sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content: Global equities were mixed but broadly firmer as cooler US inflation eased Fed-hike fears. MSCI World rose roughly **+0.7%** (approx., verify before merging) and MSCI Developed Markets a similar **+0.6%** (approx., verify before merging), while MSCI Emerging Markets outperformed at **+2.6%**, its best week since June. The S&P 500 added **0.4%** to a record **7,785.76** for a third straight weekly gain, though MAG7 leadership was patchy even as Nvidia briefly topped a **$5trn** valuation. Euro Stoxx 50 was little changed near **6,547** (approx. flat, verify before merging), China's CSI 300 firmed about **+2%** (approx., verify before merging) and Japan's Nikkei 225 surged roughly **+4.7%** to **68,714** (approx., verify before merging), while Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell around **-2.1%**.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equities eked out a third consecutive weekly advance amid a low-volatility melt-up, with the S&P 500 up **0.4%** to a record **7,785.76** and the Nasdaq Composite adding **0.1%** to **26,729.16**. Small-caps led as the Russell 2000 jumped **3.15%** to a fresh record **3,068.42**, while the Dow slipped **0.6%** to **53,732.41**, snapping a two-week run on healthcare and industrial weakness. The VIX eased to multi-month lows near **14.85**.

The pivotal catalyst was July CPI, released mid-week, showing headline inflation up just **0.1%** m/m and cooling to **3.4%** y/y from **3.5%**, with core CPI at **2.5%**. The soft print, alongside a **0.6%** drop in July retail sales and a slide in University of Michigan sentiment to **51.0**, damped fears of a September Fed hike.

Style leadership rotated toward rate-sensitive small-caps and value, while mega-cap growth was uneven; Nvidia briefly crossed a **$5trn** market value on reports of $500bn in AI datacentre orders, underscoring that AI capex remains the dominant equity narrative.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities drifted sideways to lower, with the pan-European STOXX Europe 600 slipping about **-0.2%** to **657.86** and ending a four-week winning streak, while the UK's FTSE 100 posted its first weekly decline in five weeks.

Regional dispersion was pronounced. The Euro Stoxx 50 finished roughly flat near **6,547** and Germany's DAX eased to about **26,292**, as strength in software names such as SAP and Amadeus was offset by declines in ASML, banks including HSBC, and pharmaceutical heavyweights Novartis and Roche.

The macro backdrop was supportive at the margin: softer US CPI eased global rate-hike concerns and earlier resilient tech earnings underpinned momentum. Even so, elevated long-end yields and lingering Middle East geopolitical risk capped gains and kept regional risk appetite in check into the close.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asian markets diverged sharply. Japanese equities led, with the Nikkei 225 climbing roughly **+4.7%** to about **68,714** as speculation over a nearer-term BoJ rate hike lifted financials and firmed the yen, and South Korea's KOSPI also posted powerful gains on the AI and semiconductor cycle.

Chinese equities were firmer, with the mainland CSI 300 higher on the week (approx. **+2%**, verify before merging), though Hong Kong bucked the trend: the Hang Seng retreated sharply to finish down around **-2.1%** amid profit-taking in tech and property names.

The common thread was tension between improving US rate expectations, which buoyed risk assets and lifted EM broadly, and persistent Middle East geopolitical risk that kept oil bid and tempered enthusiasm across the region.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar posted its first weekly gain in three despite softer US jobs and inflation data. The paradox reflected the curve: short-dated UST yields fell as markets judged the Fed can afford to wait, but sticky long-end yields kept the greenback supported, with the DXY firming.

The euro remained stuck in a tight range, gaining little traction from the softer-dollar narrative, while sterling was resilient but rangebound; low FX volatility offered support, yet with UK fundamentals struggling to register, GBP stayed beholden to the dollar, risk sentiment and energy prices.

The yen was the standout, strengthening roughly **4%** against the dollar over three sessions on Japan rate-hike hopes and prior intervention. Even so, the relatively contained move in USD/JPY suggested a lasting unwind of the crowded yen-short carry trade remains uncertain.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Precious metals set the tone. Gold held above **$4,400**, trading near **$4,388** and up around **1%** on the week for a monthly gain exceeding **10%**, as cooling CPI, a firmer case for Fed patience, fiscal-debt concerns and steady central-bank demand underpinned bullion, though some inflation-driven length was pared late in the week.

Energy firmed as Middle East supply risk resurfaced: Brent rose to about **$88.52** and WTI to roughly **$82.40**, with the rebound reviving inflation worries just as CPI landed and complicating the disinflation narrative.

The cross-asset read was two-sided: lower real-rate expectations supported gold and risk assets, while firmer crude lifted long-end inflation breakevens, helping steepen sovereign curves and keeping energy-sensitive currencies and equities in focus.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
Sovereign curves bear-steepened. The 10-year UST yield rose to **4.68%**, just shy of **4.70%**, and the 30-year climbed to around **5.26%**, while the 2-year eased to **4.17%** as traders concluded the Fed can wait despite soft data. The rise in long yields alongside weaker retail sales reflected Middle East uncertainty and a tick up in year-ahead inflation expectations.

With the Fed's target range at **3.50%-3.75%**, cooler July CPI at **3.4%** y/y pushed September hike odds lower, reinforcing the front-end rally even as the back end sold off and duration lagged.

Credit tone stayed constructive amid the low-volatility backdrop: IG spreads were broadly steady and HY held firm, supported by resilient risk appetite, though richer valuations and firmer oil argued for selectivity as the data-dependent outlook persisted.
